newsitem.title: FRANCE: Australia, France bury nuclear test hatchet.
newsitem.headline: Australia, France bury nuclear test hatchet.

text.p: Australia formally buried the hatchet with France on Monday in their bitter dispute over French nuclear tests in the South Pacific when visiting Defence Minister Ian McLachlan announced defence ties were restored.

"I am more than delighted to say that the relationship that had more than a dent in it last year is now completely mended," he told reporters at a joint briefing with French Defence Minister Charles Millon.
"I look forward to that relationship going forward from now on," he said.

"A few strands in our relationship were loosened over the testing issue. These have now been pulled tight. The test issue is one which we all believe now belongs in the past," McLachlan said in a statement.

McLachlan added that Australia had appointed a new defence attache to France, expected to take up his post around March, to take over a post that has been vacant since his predecessor was recalled in July 1995 in protest over the tests.
Millon echoed McLachlan, saying the controversy over France's tests "was now ancient history".

Canberra withdrew the military envoy in protest at President Jacques Chirac's decision in June 1995 to resume underground nuclear weapons tests at the Mururoa and Fangataufa atolls in French Polynesia.
After a huge international campaign spearheaded by Australia and New Zealand, the tests were concluded ahead of schedule in January. France has since committed itself to a global test ban.
Both McLachlan and Millon said they talked about defence industry relationships but neither went into details.

"There is a great opportunity to improve these relationships and to use Australia not only as a place to purchase French equipment but as a place from where we can manufacture equipment for other people," McLachlan said.

Asked if Australia might again purchase French aircraft which were a mainstay of its defences in the 1960s, McLachlan replied: "Why not? But we're not so full of money that we're buying any more aircraft just at the moment."
The backbone of the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) in the 1960s was a fleet of 72 French-made Mirage fighters and fighter-bombers, a huge contract at the time.
Millon said stability and peace in the Pacific were also discussed.
Australian diplomats said naval exchange visits between Australia and the French overseas territory of New Caledonia would also resume.
